member.name: M:MelloSilveiraTools.MechanicsOfMaterials.Optimizations.CurveFitting.Algorithms.CurveFitterBase.CalculateNumericalGradient(MelloSilveiraTools.MechanicsOfMaterials.Optimizations.CurveFitting.Models.CurveFitInput,System.Double[])
member.summary: Computes the numerical gradient of the objective function (Sum of Squared Residuals) using central finite differences with an scale-adaptive step size.
member.param: The curve fitting problem input definition.
The parameter vector at which the gradient is evaluated.
member.returns: The gradient vector containing partial derivatives with respect to each parameter.
member.remarks:
The finite difference step size h is chosen adaptively as Math.Max(1e-6, 1e-4 * |p_i|):
For small parameters (|p_i| <= 0.01): The absolute floor 1e-6 prevents underflow, division by zero, and numerical instability near the origin.
For large parameters (|p_i| >> 1, e.g. elastic modulus E ~ 1e4 or slow relaxation time tau_2 ~ 1e3 s): A fixed step like 1e-6 represents an infinitesimal relative perturbation (1e-9 or smaller), which causes catastrophic cancellation in double-precision floating-point arithmetic and leads to zero gradients, causing gradient-based optimizers (such as L-BFGS) to terminate prematurely. The proportional component (1e-4 * |p_i|) maintains a 0.01% perturbation, ensuring robust and smooth gradient estimation across diverse parameter magnitudes.

member.name: T:MelloSilveiraTools.MechanicsOfMaterials.Optimizations.ExperimentalData.Pipelines.Steps.CurveFitter.Fung.FungLogarithmicEstimator
member.summary: Provides analytical pre-estimation of the continuous Fung quasi-linear viscoelastic (QLV) reduced relaxation function parameters using logarithmic time-scale regression as formulated by Y.C. Fung (1993, Section 7.6, p. 302). Acts as the single source of truth for physical bounds and default parameter values of the Fung reduced relaxation function.

remarks.para:
Theoretical Foundation (Fung, 1993, p. 302):
In Fung's QLV theory, the reduced relaxation function is governed by a continuous spectrum S(τ) = C / τ for τ₁ ≤ τ ≤ τ₂:
G(t) = [1 + C · (E₁(t/τ₂) - E₁(t/τ₁))] / [1 + C · ln(τ₂/τ₁)]
Taking the derivative with respect to logarithmic time u = ln(t):
dG/d(ln t) = t · (dG/dt) = C · [e^(-t/τ₁) - e^(-t/τ₂)] / [1 + C · ln(τ₂/τ₁)]
In the intermediate time domain (τ₁ << t << τ₂):
e^(-t/τ₁) ≈ 0 (since t >> τ₁).
e^(-t/τ₂) ≈ 1 (since t << τ₂).
Hence, the slope in semi-logarithmic coordinates is strictly constant:
dG/d(ln t) ≈ -S = -C / [1 + C · ln(τ₂/τ₁)] ==> S > 0

Asymptotic Series and Analytical Extraction of τ₁:
Utilizing the series expansion for the exponential integral E₁(z) = -γ - ln(z) + O(z) (where γ is the Euler-Mascheroni constant, ), the intermediate relaxation function satisfies:
G(t) ≈ 1 - S · γ - S · ln(t/τ₁) = (1 - S · γ + S · ln(τ₁)) - S · ln(t) = A - S · ln(t)
Equating the linear regression intercept A = 1 - S · γ + S · ln(τ₁) yields:
ln(τ₁) = (A - 1) / S + γ ==> τ₁ = exp((A - 1) / S + γ)

Soft Tissue Testing Reality and Asymmetry of τ₂:
Experimental tension/relaxation tests on knee ligaments and soft tissues cannot be maintained indefinitely without tissue desiccation, enzymatic degradation, and clamping slippage. Standard laboratory protocols terminate after t_max ~ 400 - 1600 s, while the specimen is still in the linear logarithmic decay phase (τ₁ << t << τ₂). Therefore, the long-term knee at t ~ τ₂ (τ₂ ~ 10³ - 10⁵ s) is never observed experimentally.
Consequently, this estimator:
Extracts S and τ₁ analytically from the initial transition and linear logarithmic decay.
Initializes τ₂⁰ = max(1000.0, 3.0 · t_max) to strictly exceed experimental duration.
Deduces the consistent relaxation stiffness C⁰ = S / [1 - S · ln(τ₂⁰ / τ₁)].
These parameters provide an adaptive, physically grounded warm-start for numerical optimizers (e.g., L-BFGS), drastically accelerating convergence and eliminating sensitivity to arbitrary initial guesses.
